source: Fiddick, Cosmides & Tooby (2000) No interpretation without representation: domain-specific representations and inferences in the Wason selection task
finding: Defence of social contract and hazard-management algorithms against relevance theory. Removing the if-then wording did not hurt cheater selections much. Precaution (hazard) rules raised correct P and not-Q even though they were descriptive, not deontic.
numbers: Exp1 (N=60, 30 per group): P&not-Q 67% Conditional vs 50% Want version (no connective), Z=1.31, not significant. Exp2 (N=60): precaution rule 50% P&not-Q vs standard rule 17%, Z=2.74, p<.004. Exp3 (N=120): same poison-dart rule gave 70% P&not-Q when asked about risk, only 5% when asked about abusing a privilege (58% chose not-P&Q instead).
quote: the results support the predictions of social contract theory and hazard management theory
limits: Authors' own lab. The cheater question is posed in the task wording, which Sperber and Girotto say turns it into a categorisation task. Small cells (30 per group).
agent_relevance: What counts as the right check depends on which goal the problem states (find cheaters, find rule violations, find risk). The scaffold should restate the goal in one plain sentence before choosing what to test.

source: Fiddick, Cosmides & Tooby (2000) No interpretation without representation: domain-specific representations and inferences in the Wason selection task
finding: Reports an older result as context: Gigerenzer and Hug (1992) found the same social-contract rule gives P&not-Q when you are cued as employee, but not-P&Q when cued as employer. The cheating version gave almost twice the P&not-Q rate of the no-cheating version, which was about as low as descriptive rules.
numbers: 'almost twice as many' P&not-Q for cheating vs no-cheating versions (Gigerenzer and Hug 1992; exact figures not given in this paper). Abstract-rule P&not-Q 'less than 10%' of subjects, as quoted from earlier work.
limits: Second-hand summary of Gigerenzer and Hug, not the original. The perspective effect fits cheater detection and also fits a relevance or interpretation account (Sperber et al. 1995).
agent_relevance: Same rule, different role in the story, different correct-looking answer. The agent should fix whose viewpoint a check is run from, and test it on a role-swapped copy of the item.

source: Sperber & Girotto (2002) Use or misuse of the selection task? Rejoinder to Fiddick, Cosmides, and Tooby
finding: Argues that the cheater-detection evidence mixes two questions: the true Wason question (was the rule obeyed?) and a trivial categorisation question (which card might show a cheater?). With a neutral made-up category people did even better than with cheaters.
numbers: Exp1 (N=100, Trieste students, 35/35/30): P&not-Q 68% look-for-cheater, 91% look-for-arbitrary-category ('Wason's selection'), 73% look-for-glider. Cheater vs arbitrary chi2(1,N=70)=4.37, p<.05. A replication of the glider group (N=20) gave 65%.
quote: cheaters are not more easily detected than arbitrary items such as Wason's selections
limits: Italian humanities students. The cheater condition (68%) scored below the arbitrary condition even though both defining traits were stated; the authors call this puzzling.
agent_relevance: If the instruction names the target category and its two defining traits, the task is easy whatever the content. Spelling out 'violation = P and not-Q' is a cheap input fix.

source: Sperber & Girotto (2002) Use or misuse of the selection task? Rejoinder to Fiddick, Cosmides, and Tooby
finding: Exp2 changed only the final instruction, from 'see whether anyone cheated you' to 'see whether anyone made an exchange with you'. Card choice followed the instruction, not the exchange scenario. It is also a partial failed replication of Fiddick et al. Exp1.
numbers: Exp2 (N=120, 30 per cell): P&not-Q 33% (cheater, conditional) and 43% (cheater, want) vs 10% and 0% under exchange wording. P&Q was 33% and 53% under exchange wording. Fiddick et al. had 67% and 50%; the conditional-version result did not replicate (33% vs 66%), 'no confident explanation'.
limits: Students, one scenario (potatoes and corn), cells of 30. The authors do not claim cheater detection is false.
agent_relevance: Strong sign that models and people answer the question asked. The agent must restate the exact question (violation vs cheating vs exchange) before choosing tests.

source: Sperber & Girotto (2002) Use or misuse of the selection task? Rejoinder to Fiddick, Cosmides, and Tooby
finding: Relevance manipulations can flip performance in both directions: a descriptive rule made easy and a deontic rule made hard by story context alone. Also a re-reading of Cosmides 1989 Big Kiku tasks, where answers fit the cheating question and not the rule.
numbers: Cited from Sperber, Cara & Girotto 1995 and Girotto, Kemmelmeier, Sperber & van der Henst 2001: descriptive versions pushed above 50% correct; deontic versions pushed to over 80% incorrect. Cosmides 1989 Big Kiku: 71% (Exp2) and 75% (Exp4, switched rule).
limits: Cited results, not re-run here. The Big Kiku reading is the authors' interpretation.
agent_relevance: Content effects are not a fixed bonus for social content. Surface framing steers which reading of the rule the solver adopts.

source: Sperber & Girotto (2003) Does the selection task detect cheater-detection?
finding: Review of relevance-theory predictions. A descriptive rule that denies a salient combination was solved by most people; a matched control by few. A deontic rule described as no longer in force gave the usual descriptive error.
numbers: Prince descriptive task: 70% correct (P and not-Q) vs 25% for the matched control. Cholera travel rule: 62% P&not-Q when the rule was in force; 15% P&not-Q and 71% P&Q when it was said to be no longer in force (Girotto et al. 2001). Baseline: over 80% fail standard descriptive versions; over 50% correct on standard deontic.
limits: Cited from earlier studies; sample sizes not given in the text I read.
agent_relevance: The same words with the same logic give opposite answers depending on whether the rule is live. Checks must be tied to what the rule is for, which the agent can state in S1.

source: Sperber & Girotto (2003) Does the selection task detect cheater-detection?
finding: New experiments separating the real Wason question from the cheater question. The cheating question pulls toward cheater cards; the genuine Wason question pulls toward P&Q or P&not-Q. A genuine deontic task with no benefit-requirement structure still gave P&not-Q about half the time.
numbers: Exp1 (N=60): Wason version majority P&Q (or P,Q,not-Q), none chose P&not-Q; Wason/FCT version majority P&not-Q, none P&Q; chi2(1,N=60)=19.9 and 23.3, p<.001. Exp2A (N=60): P&Q 50% vs 13%, p<.01; P&not-Q 17% vs 47%, p<.05. Exp3 law 'condemned person must carry ID': 47% P&not-Q, 0% P&Q.
limits: Same Trieste lab as the 2002 paper, about 30 people per cell. Not an independent replication.
agent_relevance: A deontic framing helps even without a benefit-cost structure, so social contract is not required. Supports the simpler claim: tell the solver what a violation is.

source: Ragni & Johnson-Laird (2020) Explanation or modeling: a reply to Kellen and Klauer
finding: Meta-analysis of 228 selection-task experiments (Ragni, Kola & Johnson-Laird 2018) kept the old model theory and eliminated all but one of 15 rival theories. The survivor, the inference-guessing theory, has more free parameters. Kellen and Klauer dispute the diagnostic value of the tests.
numbers: 228 experiments, 16 theories compared on three predictions: canonical selections, dependence among card choices, salience of counterexamples. Original abstract-task selections: pq 46%, p 33%, pq-bar 7%, other 4%. Online studies (N=3787) had more idiosyncratic selections (median 2.67 bits, p<.0002). Repeated-selection study at the end: 53% partial insight, 31% correct.
quote: no findings from the 228 experiments appear to be either so large or so robust
limits: Written by the model theory's own authors, as a reply to a critic. The meta-analysis targets the abstract task, not content effects directly. The debate is unresolved.
agent_relevance: No single theory of the task is settled, so the agent should not hard-code one account of why content helps. Counterexample salience is the one effect the authors report as corroborated.

source: Ragni & Johnson-Laird (2020) Explanation or modeling: a reply to Kellen and Klauer
finding: The meta-analysis predicts that making counterexamples salient raises correct selections, and says this is corroborated. The authors also say no effect in the 228 experiments is very large.
numbers: Ten of the other theories fail the salience prediction. Effect size is not stated in the reply; it sits in Ragni et al. 2018 Table 4, which I did not open.
limits: Magnitude unknown. Reply paper only.
agent_relevance: Supports an operator that writes out the concrete falsifying case for the current rule before testing. The size is unknown, so test it at equal tokens (G7).

source: Klauer, Stahl & Erdfelder (2007) The abstract selection task: new data and an almost comprehensive model
finding: A model that explains all 16 response patterns on the abstract task. About 75% of responses come from inference and about 25% from independent card-by-card guessing. Only a small share of inference responses use reversible reasoning (taking the hidden side into account).
numbers: 18 data sets; six experiments of about 300 participants each, run online. The inference-guessing model fitted 16 of 18 data sets at the 5% level (e.g. G2(10)=10.85, p=.37 and 5.87, p=.83). Parameter a about 75%; independence about 25%; about 10% of inference responses reversible. Correct P&not-Q 'typically fewer than 10%'.
limits: Abstract task only. Model complexity is a standing complaint (Ragni and Johnson-Laird).
agent_relevance: Most failure is shallow one-way reading plus noise. Prompting the solver to check each card's hidden side is the targeted fix.

source: Klauer, Stahl & Erdfelder (2007) The abstract selection task: new data and an almost comprehensive model
finding: Instruction hints worked only partly. A hint to consider every hidden possibility for each card lowered the irreversibility parameter. Raw correct selections rose modestly. The three-hint version cut P&Q selections strongly.
numbers: Exp1: one hint vs control; Exp2: three hints vs control. Descriptively a modest increase in P&not-Q in both; parameter i significantly reduced in both (chi-square tests of group difference). Exact percentages per group not captured.
quote: the hints led to a modest increase in (p, not-q) selections in both experiments
limits: Exact percent correct per group not captured in my read. Hints did not raise correct performance to a high level.
agent_relevance: A plain procedural hint (for each card, list what could be on the other side) helps a little. Expect small gains from wording alone.

source: Lampinen, Dasgupta et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: Models and humans tested on NLI, syllogisms and the Wason task. The content effect grows with task difficulty: small on NLI, clear on syllogisms, and on Wason both humans and models do better with realistic rules than with arbitrary or nonsense ones.
numbers: Models: Chinchilla, PaLM 2 (several sizes), Flan-PaLM 2, GPT-3.5. Syllogism content effect significant for humans and all models (all z>=2.25). Wason realistic advantage: Chinchilla, PaLM 2-L, GPT-3.5 and humans all z>2.2, p<0.03; PaLM 2-M and Flan-PaLM 2 marginal (z about 1.78, p about 0.08). Humans on Wason not above chance overall.
limits: Crowd-worker humans; forced choice of two cards; models scored by likelihood with a correction, not free text. Error patterns differ from humans on Wason.
agent_relevance: Content effects in models are real and shrink as the underlying logic gets easier. Test the agent on content-swapped copies of items to measure its own bias.

source: Lampinen, Dasgupta et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: Slow human responders show content effects too: on the Wason task they are above chance only on realistic items. Longer response time predicts accuracy.
numbers: Human Wason accuracy vs response time: z=4.44, p<0.001 (logistic regression). Slowest 15% (over 80 s) above chance for Realistic, near chance for other conditions. A second sample with a performance bonus: no significant difference in accuracy or content effects.
limits: The slow/fast split is post hoc. Response time is confounded with ability and effort.
agent_relevance: Extra deliberation alone does not remove content effects in people. It did help strong models when prompted well (next line).

source: Lampinen, Dasgupta et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: Prompt interventions: few-shot gives mild gains and leaves content effects in place. Chain-of-thought can move a strong model from strong content bias to fairly high accuracy on arbitrary and nonsense Wason items, if the examples show the needed reasoning.
numbers: Qualitative in the main text; exact CoT accuracies are in the supplement, not read. Few-shot: mild improvements, larger on easier tasks.
limits: Exact CoT gains not read. Strong model only; weaker models gain less.
agent_relevance: CoT with a worked pattern can cut content bias for a strong model. Code can also compare the answer on the original and the abstracted copy and flag disagreement.

source: Bertolazzi, Pezzelle & Bernardi (2025) How language models conflate logical validity with plausibility: a representational analysis of content effects
finding: In open models the valid direction and the plausible direction are linearly encoded and aligned. Models with more alignment show larger content effects. Adding a vector that removes the plausibility part cut the content effect to near zero. CoT alone also removes most of it.
numbers: Cosine similarity of validity and plausibility vectors 0.48 to 0.64, vs 0.10 to 0.13 and -0.12 to -0.17 for control concepts. Content effect (CE): Qwen2.5-32B 0.348 zero-shot to 0.096 with CoT; Qwen3-14B 0.213 to 0.014 with CoT. Debias vector: Qwen2.5-32B accuracy 81.62 to 82.21 and CE 0.348 to 0.072; Qwen3-14B accuracy 86.54 to 96.70 and CE 0.213 to 0.043. Across Qwen2.5, Qwen3, Gemma-3: zero-shot CE 0.063 to 0.418; CoT CE -0.006 to 0.147 with accuracy over 89%.
limits: Preprint, open-weight models, one synthetic syllogism set (64 premise combinations). Activation steering is not available to our scaffold.
agent_relevance: CoT is the lever we can use, and it removes most of the effect for these models. We cannot steer activations, so we mimic it by also showing the model a content-neutral copy.

source: Eisape et al. (2024) A systematic comparison of syllogistic reasoning in humans and language models
finding: With content kept near neutral (30 word triples with minimal semantic association), larger PaLM 2 models beat humans on syllogisms but still show human-like order and fallacy errors. They almost never answer 'nothing follows'.
numbers: Human mean accuracy about 50%; best LM about 75%; scale does not always help. 'Nothing follows' accuracy near 0% for LMs. Zero-shot CoT prompt, 30 samples per syllogism per content triple, temperature 0.5. Llama 2 accuracy similar to humans.
limits: Content was deliberately neutralised, so this tests form biases (figure order, fallacies) rather than belief effects. Main result is one model family.
agent_relevance: Neutral content removes belief bias but not form-based errors. Abstraction alone is not a full cure, so keep a code-side validity check for syllogism-like items.

source: Ando et al. (2023) Evaluating large language models with NeuBAROCO: syllogistic reasoning ability and human-like biases
finding: On a bilingual syllogism set, belief-inconsistent items were the hardest for every model, and GPT-3.5 did equally well on symbolic and belief-consistent items. Conversion and atmosphere errors also appeared.
numbers: Dataset: 95 symbolic, 167 consistent, 102 inconsistent items. GPT-3.5 accuracy: symbolic 61.05%, consistent 56.89%, inconsistent 31.37%. RoBERTa 24.21/46.11/22.55%. BART 34.74/45.51/15.69%. GPT-3.5 overall 51.73%; conversion-error items 25.71%; atmosphere items 39.42%.
limits: Older models (GPT-3.5, RoBERTa, BART); three-way label task; symbolic and consistent items differ in other ways too.
agent_relevance: Belief-inconsistent content cost about 25 to 30 points against abstract content for a mid-size model. Use abstract copies as an input check on items with surprising content.

source: Abe et al. (2026) Evaluation of deontic conditional reasoning in large language models: the case of Wason's selection task
finding: Models do better on deontic than descriptive Wason rules across all models and prompts, and recent reasoning models reach near ceiling on deontic. Errors on deontic rules fit matching bias better than confirmation bias.
numbers: Deontic minus descriptive: +5.0 to +41.2 points across all models and prompts. Zero-shot deontic accuracy: gpt-oss-120b 100.0 (+30), qwen3-14b 97.5 (+45), gpt-oss-20b 67.5 (+27.5; few-shot 91.2, +41.2). Nine open models including Gemma 3, Llama 3.3 70B, OLMo 2 32B.
limits: Open models only, preprint. Deontic modality is encoded in wording, so effects may come from wording cues. Reasoning models had no CoT condition.
agent_relevance: Strong reasoning models still show the deontic gap. Checking a negated or reworded copy of the rule tests for matching bias.

source: Mirzadeh et al. (2024) GSM-Symbolic: understanding the limitations of mathematical reasoning in large language models
finding: Changing only names and numbers in grade-school maths problems lowers accuracy and widens variance. Adding one irrelevant but plausible clause causes large drops. A close analogue of content sensitivity in a maths task.
numbers: 50 sets generated from 100 templates, 8-shot CoT. Changing names gave smaller variance than changing numbers. GSM-NoOp (one irrelevant clause): drops up to 65% across state-of-the-art models; using examples of the same question as shots did not recover the loss.
limits: Maths, not logic. Per-model averages sit in figures I did not transcribe.
agent_relevance: A single distracting clause is a content effect. Strip clauses no step uses and re-solve; flag disagreement.

source: Wu et al. (2023) Reasoning or reciting? Exploring the capabilities and limitations of language models through counterfactual tasks
finding: On 11 tasks, models do above chance when the rules are changed but fall consistently below the default version. Same pattern as content effects: reliance on familiar versions.
numbers: 11 tasks; GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude, PaLM-2. Counterfactual accuracy above random but below default on every task. Zero-shot CoT usually helped but sometimes hurt (PaLM-2 base-10 and base-16 addition).
limits: Only the abstract, intro and conclusions were read; per-task numbers not captured.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a pass on the familiar form. Re-test on a counterfactual form (G3: something the answer was not fitted to).

source: Stanovich & West (1998) Cognitive ability and variation in selection task performance
finding: Higher cognitive ability goes with better abstract (non-deontic) selection task performance. Two deontic problems (drinking-age, Sears) showed no link with ability.
numbers: Over 800 participants in three experiments (from a search summary, not the paper).
limits: Not opened: only a search summary seen. A 2004 QJEP paper reportedly found no ability link in two of three experiments, and the link only among higher-ability people.
agent_relevance: Weaker analytic reasoners gain most from familiar content. The agent equivalent: a strong model needs less help, so check per model.

source: Cosmides (1989) The logic of social exchange; Cheng & Holyoak (1985) Pragmatic reasoning schemas; Griggs & Cox (1982)
finding: The founding content-effect results: social-exchange rules with cheater framing gave far higher P&not-Q than matched abstract rules; Cheng and Holyoak's permission schemas explain gains for permission rules; the drinking-age rule is the classic big gain.
numbers: Only second-hand: Cosmides 1989 Big Kiku Exp2 71% and Exp4 75% (as quoted in Sperber & Girotto 2002).
limits: Originals not read. The Cheng-Holyoak versus Cosmides contest (permission schema vs social contract) is known here only via Fiddick et al. footnotes.
agent_relevance: Placeholder so primary sources are tracked. Do not cite their numbers as read.

source: Sperber, Cara & Girotto (1995) Relevance theory explains the selection task
finding: Relevance-guided comprehension decides card choice in most versions, so the task tests comprehension more than reasoning. Descriptive versions can be pushed above 50% correct.
numbers: Second-hand via Sperber & Girotto 2002 and 2003: more than 50% correct for relevance-manipulated descriptive tasks.
limits: Original not opened.
agent_relevance: Rival to the evolved-module account. Both predict a content effect; they diverge on the in-force and which-question manipulations above.

source: Kellen & Klauer (2020) critique of Ragni et al. 2018, Computational Brain & Behavior
finding: Critique of the 228-experiment meta-analysis: the model theory is non-identifiable and often fails to fit the data, and the diagnostic value of its predictions is limited.
numbers: None captured; described in the Ragni and Johnson-Laird reply and in a search summary.
limits: Not opened; only the reply was read.
agent_relevance: Keeps the one-winning-theory idea of the selection task open.

source: Cheater-detection critiques: Fiddick & Rutherford (2006); a 2005 study of cheater-detection contexts; altruism-detection study (2010)
finding: Search-summary level only. Cheater detection was found even without losses. One study found altruism-detection results depended on the answer being embedded in the scenario (cheater versions were unaffected). A 2005 paper found performance could not be predicted from cheater-detection context alone.
numbers: No numbers retrieved.
limits: From search summaries, not the papers. Findings point in different directions.
agent_relevance: Shows the rival claims remain open. Do not build anything that hinges on cheater detection being a module.
